correctness.rationale: For every fixed x,y, the exact cyclic chord-ratio map z↦q increases strictly from zero to one with explicitly positive derivative. Under x=epsilon^u, q=epsilon v, z∼4epsilon v sin²(y/2)/x on every interior triple 0<u,v<1 and 0<y<2pi. The Dirichlet constant density 3/(4pi³) and exact Jacobian give pointwise unconditioned density 3epsilon log(1/epsilon)sin²(y/2)/pi³. The known normalized scalar cross-ratio density from Martin integrates to one and yields event probability (3/pi²)epsilon log(1/epsilon)(1+o(1)); the conditional pointwise limit sin²(y/2)/pi integrates to one. Scheffe yields L¹/TV convergence, and root azimuth is independent uniform at every epsilon. This is an infinite-dimensional-asymptotic proof; the embedded checker is supporting finite numerical evidence only.

originality.rationale: The claimed original output is the four-dimensional conditional marked total-variation law, NOT the known marginal distribution or its logarithmic cusp. Martin (2018), Theorem 4.1, gives the latter, not the conditional law of two angular collision scales or their sine-square-biased separation. Vuorinen–Wang (2012), Izmestiev (2014), and Wang–Vuorinen–Zhang (2019) give deterministic ideal quadrilateral/cyclic cross-ratio geometry, not this stochastic marked limit. The closest compared published five-vertex joint cross-ratio tail involves two ratios and a Cauchy-coordinate residue; it does not imply the fixed-four-vertex Dirichlet angular marks. Priority remains provisional.
residual_risks: Classical Dirichlet product-tail conditioning and older unindexed probabilistic cross-ratio literature could conceivably contain the same marked statement.
The angular marks are sampling-frame-dependent and not individual Möbius invariants; no claim of Möbius-invariant marked law.
No independent mathematical audit; exact finite-threshold marked density is not claimed.

value.rationale: The boundary-cusp of random ideal quadrilaterals is a natural geometric degeneration linked to punctured-torus cross-ratio moduli. The known 1D cusp probability cannot say whether rare small cross ratios arise from a single collision or two separated collisions, what scales they occupy, or where the resulting pair of clusters lies on the circle. The theorem resolves all three structural questions jointly: two paired collisions, a uniform logarithmic split, a sine-square-biased cluster separation, and independent normalized overshoot. The precise mark distribution offers a meaningful geometric refinement rather than a renamed scalar table or arbitrary numerical slice.
